design: cross-sectional | global multilingual online survey (responses collected May 2022-August 2023 by convenience sampling)
N_total: received 2955 ; analysed 1352 ; with complete taste and smell data 1220
population_description: Adults aged 18 years or older who had received a COVID-19 vaccine, with and without pre-existing COVID-19-related chemosensory impairment before vaccination; most aged 25-64 years (71.6%); 46.99% identified as cis women
taste_types_reported: unspecified taste dysfunction; dysgeusia (reported as distorted taste, assessed as a single category; paper states it did not distinguish between specific qualitative gustatory disorders)
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no / self-reported change (improved, worsened or no change after each vaccine dose, in online survey)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Pre-vaccination chemosensory impairments due to COVID-19 reported by 599 of 1220 participants with complete taste and smell data (49%); of these 416 reported impairments in both smell and taste; pre-vaccination distorted taste reported by 380 participants (no % printed for that count)
onset_timing: Among the 75 participants who reported timing and duration of post-vaccination chemosensory changes, approximately two-thirds indicated onset occurred on the day following vaccination and most reported symptom duration longer than 1 month (post-vaccination changes, not initial taste-loss onset)
pathogenesis_finding: The biological mechanisms underlying post-vaccination changes remain uncertain; previous reports proposed transient inflammatory responses within the olfactory neuroepithelium or immune-mediated effects related to residual viral material following SARS-CoV-2 infection, and the authors state these mechanisms remain speculative and the observational design precludes mechanistic inference
special_populations_notes: Pregnancy: respondents pregnant after the outbreak of COVID were excluded (n=69), pregnancy described as a known modulator of chemosensory ability; children excluded (<18 years, n=33); pre-existing conditions excluded (n=228: neurological/psychiatric pathologies, head and neck trauma, nasal sinus surgery, head and neck radiation, impaired smell and taste perception)
funding_conflicts: Funding: not reported (no separate funding statement printed; Acknowledgments: Liang-Dar Hwang supported by Australian Research Council Early Discovery Researcher Award (DE240100014)). Conflicts: Kathrin Ohla works at dsm-firmenich, company had no influence on study design or interpretation; other authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): design coded cross-sectional per R1(b) (single survey with denominator, no follow-up over time). Post-vaccination improvement is not labelled recovery by the paper, so per R3 it is NOT entered as recovery: improvement in distorted taste reported by 12%-21% depending on vaccine dose; among participants with pre-existing impairment 3%-8% reported improvement in smell or taste depending on dose; distorted taste after first dose 43 of 339 (12.7%) improved and 9 (2.7%) worsened (Table 3). Verbatim: 'More than 90% of participants reported no change in general smell or taste following vaccination'; 'The survey assessed distorted taste as a single category and did not distinguish between specific qualitative gustatory disorders.' Vaccination is the exposure studied; no treatment intervention for taste dysfunction was tested, so Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: cross-sectional | retrospective cross-sectional analysis of de-identified surveillance data (paper's wording)
country_setting: Panama; San Miguelito Health Region (Region de Salud de San Miguelito); surveillance / telephone follow-up data
N_total: source database 26461 unverified operational records ; received de-identified extract 6696 ; analysed 5348 (after excluding 140 aged <=5 years, 1198 non-Pfizer/mixed vaccination, 10 indeterminate vaccination category)
population_description: COVID-19-positive patients over five years of age followed by the San Miguelito Health Region from July 7 2021 through November 2 2022; mean age 47.36 +/- 21.31 years; age groups 6-17, 18-29, 30-62 and 63 years or older; unvaccinated or exclusively Pfizer-BioNTech vaccinated
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (self-reported ageusia during telephone follow-up call)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia was reported by 507 patients (9.48%); by vaccine dose: 192 with zero doses (17.50%), 99 with one dose (27.35%), 171 with two doses (9.90%), and 45 with three to four doses (2.08%)
special_populations_notes: Children: age group 6-17 years n=556 (10.40%) included, patients aged five years or younger excluded (n=140); older adults: age group 63+ n=1538 (28.76%); diabetes recorded in 464 patients (8.68%); chronic kidney disease 14 (0.26%); immunosuppression 17 (0.32%)
follow_up_duration: not reported (single first follow-up call; data July 7 2021-November 2 2022)
funding_conflicts: Funding: all authors declared no financial support was received from any organization for the submitted work. Conflicts: no financial relationships or other relationships that might have an interest in the submitted work (ICMJE disclosures)
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): virus_confirmation = laboratory-confirmed (assay not stated) per R7(a) — patients are described as COVID-19-positive with swab dates recorded (swab dates July 5 2021-October 31 2022) but no assay is named; extractor B's 'not reported' does not apply under R7(a). Primary adjusted (Model III) ageusia aORs vs two doses: zero doses 1.87 (95% CI 1.48-2.38), one dose 2.68 (95% CI 1.99-3.60), three to four doses 0.26 (95% CI 0.18-0.36); after categorical adjustment for swab month none remained statistically significant. No pathogenesis mechanism was proposed or tested by this study itself (discussion cites Huhn et al. on antibody responses and ACE2 neutralization as biological context only; general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended — not Q2-coded per R5), so Q2 fields blank. Vaccine dose category is an exposure, not a treatment for taste dysfunction, so Q3 fields blank per R6.

country_setting: Brazil; single centre: Interdisciplinary Laboratory for Health Promotion Intervention (LIIPS), Unicesumar, Maringa, Parana
population_description: Post-COVID-19 individuals aged 19-65 years referred after hospital discharge in Maringa; contracted COVID-19 between March 1 and July 1 2021; mean age 47.7 +/- 12.8 years; 105 (52.2%) male; all had received at least the first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine; 65 (32.3%) not hospitalised, 66 (32.8%) ward, 70 (34.8%) ICU
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (standardized questionnaire, dichotomous yes/no self-report; paper states no objective olfactory or gustatory testing was performed)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Ageusia group n=121 and no-ageusia group n=80 (of 201 total; no overall % for ageusia printed in text/tables)
onset_timing: not reported (mean time from acute COVID-19 infection to assessment was 214.5 +/- 116.4 days; symptoms asked as present during acute phase, after hospital discharge, or both)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Duration-of-ageusia categories as printed in Table 3, among the 121 with ageusia: <2 months n=93 (<12wk — not >=12wk persistence); 2-4 months n=11; 4-6 months n=5; >6 months n=12; no >=12-week proportion printed
pathogenesis_finding: Ageusia was independently associated with memory deficit (adjusted OR = 2.91; 95% CI 1.47-5.75) and aural fullness (adjusted OR = 4.08; 95% CI 1.02-16.30) but not with VO2peak, which the authors interpret as consistent with central neuroinflammatory involvement rather than cardiorespiratory mechanisms
special_populations_notes: Diabetes mellitus 32 (15.9%) in cohort; exclusion criteria were debilitating neurological diseases or mobility limitations requiring a cane or wheelchair; age restricted to 19-65 years as stated (no children or older adults over 65)
follow_up_duration: not reported (cross-sectional, no longitudinal follow-up; lack of longitudinal follow-up stated as a limitation)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Article Processing Charge funded by Coordenacao de Aperfeicoamento de Pessoal de Nivel Superior - Brasil (CAPES); study supported by Cesumar University (UniCesumar), Cesumar Institute of Science Technology and Innovation (ICETI), Araucaria Foundation PPSUS and CNPq, and a research productivity grant for the last author (Araucaria Foundation). Conflicts: authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): onset_timing = not reported — the 214.5-day figure is infection-to-assessment time, not symptom onset (extractor A had entered it as onset). Persistent field records the Table 3 duration bands exactly as printed per R4; no >=12wk proportion is printed. Verbatim: 'Anosmia, ageusia, and the neurological symptoms investigated were self-reported by the participants; no objective olfactory or gustatory testing was performed.' Pathogenesis per R5: only mechanisms the discussion extends to the ageusia finding are coded (T5 cytokine/inflammatory effects; T9 central neuroinflammatory interpretation); extractor A's T8 (vascular) derives from general post-acute cerebrovascular background not extended to taste — not coded. No mechanism was tested in this cohort, so directness is speculative. No intervention tested, Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: other (genome-wide machine learning analysis of two COVID-19 cohorts: whole genome sequencing, variant and gene prioritization)
country_setting: United States of America; University of Iowa cohort (Iowa City) and NIH All of Us Research Program cohort
N_total: UI cohort 187 ; AoU cohort 947 (no combined total printed)
population_description: Individuals in the UI COVID-19 cohort (N=187; recruited 30 June 2020 to 31 July 2022; patients under four years of age excluded; no documented history of olfactory or gustatory dysfunction prior to COVID-19) and the AoU Research Program COVID-19 cohort (N=947) with genome sequencing data, classified as cases/controls for loss of smell, loss of taste, and loss of smell and/or taste phenotypes
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (binary phenotype derived from yes/no survey responses or electronic medical records; paper states this in limitations)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: UI cohort: 8 reporting only a loss of taste, 87 reporting a loss in smell and taste, and 9 reporting only a loss of smell; in total 95 cases and 92 controls for the loss of taste phenotype (of 187). AoU cohort (combined phenotype only): 421 cases and 526 controls for loss of smell or taste (of 947)
pathogenesis_finding: Machine learning prioritized candidate host genetic factors for loss of taste including AKR1C2 (top variant feature), GRIN3A and Y RNA (top gene features), with top pathways involved in immune response, neuronal signaling and calcium signaling supporting previously proposed hypotheses for anosmia/ageusia in COVID-19 (T11: host genetic susceptibility)
special_populations_notes: Children: patients under four years of age at consent excluded from the UI cohort; minors participated with parent/guardian consent (saliva collection kits for minors described). Paper states assessment of covariates revealed no association of sex, age and age-squared with the response variable for any phenotype in the UI cohort; in the AoU cohort sex (p=0.000367), age and age-squared (p<2e-16) were associated with the response variable
funding_conflicts: Funding: University of Iowa Interdisciplinary Genetics T32 Predoctoral Training Grant T32 GM 008629 (LP), Integrated DNA Technologies Bioinformatics Fellowship Program (LP), University of Iowa Stead Family Department of Pediatrics departmental funds (HE, BD) and start-up funds for Hatem El-Shanti; funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of manuscript. Conflicts: authors have declared that no competing interests exist
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): virus_confirmation = mixed per R7(e) — UI cohort: positive infection by antibody or PCR testing OR presumed positive (symptomatic, household contact tested positive); AoU cases required self-reported positive COVID-19 test. Taste-ambiguous resolution: UI cohort analysed loss of taste separately, but AoU cohort analysed only the combined 'loss of smell and/or taste' phenotype (AoU survey symptom option was 'Loss of smell or taste'), so no taste-specific prevalence exists for AoU. Introduction verbatim: 'The most probable cause of the loss of taste with COVID-19 is the viral invasion of gustatory nerves, taste receptor cells, and the olfactory epithelium' plus pro-inflammatory cytokine damage (T1/T3/T5, cited hypotheses); the study's own evidence is host-genetic (T11), direct-human, hence directness mixed-as-stated. No treatment was tested, so Q3 fields blank per R6 ('Q3-tagged, no intervention tested').

design: prospective cohort | prospective cohort study (as stated); questionnaire four years after symptom onset, following earlier follow-up rounds
N_total: invited 697 ; responded 363 ; analysed 356 (6 excluded for different e-mail address and 1 excluded as <18 years at baseline)
population_description: Individuals aged >=18 years with sudden chemosensory dysfunction (CD) after 27 February 2020 (first confirmed Danish case); median age at enrolment 46 (range: 18-87, IQR: 36-55); 72% female as stated in Discussion; cohort defined by sudden CD during the COVID-19 pandemic
taste_measurement: patient-reported scale named: questionnaire using validated self-report items (self-reported CD/GD recovery; WHO-5 instrument for mental well-being); paper states study relied entirely on self-reported data with no psychophysical measurement of olfactory or gustatory function
taste_prevalence_as_printed: not reported for taste specifically (cohort was enrolled on the basis of sudden chemosensory dysfunction; most participants reported combined olfactory dysfunction (OD) and GD; no taste-specific numerator/denominator or % printed in the main text)
onset_timing: not reported for taste specifically (sudden CD after 27 February 2020 was an eligibility criterion; mean time from symptom onset to the baseline questionnaire was 82 days (IQR: 28-103), for CD overall)
recovery_complete_as_printed: Full GD recovery at four years by sex as printed: male participants 59% achieved full GD recovery compared with 51% of females (p=0.028). Composite CD: only 43% reported full recovery of CD after four years; 152 (43%) reported full subjective recovery
recovery_any_as_printed: not reported for taste specifically (participants reporting partial recovery or no improvement formed the composite 'Persistent CD' group; no taste-specific any/partial recovery proportion printed)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported for taste specifically (composite persistent CD at four years — i.e. >=12wk time point, CD composite: proportion reporting persistent CD was 68.3% in age 45-59 years, 52.4% in 30-44 years, 49.1% in >=60 years and 45.3% in 18-29 years)
pathogenesis_finding: Authors note as a limitation that reported taste loss may reflect impaired flavour perception rather than true gustatory dysfunction, i.e. olfactory-mediated misattribution (T4), and that validated methods such as taste strips and Sniffin' Sticks would be needed; no mechanism was tested
special_populations_notes: Older adults: subgroup aged >=60 years had persistent CD in 49.1% (composite CD); age 45-59 subgroup highest at 68.3%; children excluded (<18 years; one participant excluded for being <18 at baseline); no pregnancy/diabetes/CKD-specific results stated
follow_up_duration: Four years after symptom onset; mean follow-up was 1496 days (IQR: 1398-1616); current questionnaire distributed October 2024
funding_conflicts: Funding: None (as printed in abstract). Conflicts: AWF reports financial support from or interest in Region Midtjyllands Sundhedsvidenskabelige Forskningsfond, Folkeuniversitetet; all authors submitted ICMJE disclosure forms
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): TASTE-AMBIGUOUS record — headline outcomes are composite chemosensory dysfunction (CD = OD + GD); the only taste-specific outcome in the main text is full GD recovery by sex (59% males, 51% females). Virus confirmation mixed per R7(e): most participants had test-verified COVID-19 but lack of testing was not an exclusion criterion; PCR-confirmed group n=221 (62%) compared with no positive PCR n=135 (38%). Verbatim: 'This study relied entirely on self-reported data, with no psychophysical measurement of olfactory or gustatory function.' Treatments discussed are from other studies only, so Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: prospective cohort | one-year longitudinal cohort study (as stated in title); participants enrolled at 3, 6 or 12 months after viral clearance and re-evaluated three months later
country_setting: Hong Kong SAR, China; Hong Kong Polytechnic University; community recruitment
N_total: recruited 120 (Group 1: 40 at 3 months post-recovery, Group 2: 40 at 6 months, Group 3: 40 at 12 months) ; blood samples from 107 consented participants
virus_confirmation: laboratory-confirmed (rapid antigen (lateral flow) test or PCR)
population_description: SARS-CoV-2 survivors recruited from the community; age 59.9 +/- 8.6 years; 84 females and 36 males; all reported being symptom-free at enrolment; confirmed neurodegenerative diseases and blood-borne diseases excluded
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia (participants categorised as normogeusia group or hypogeusia/ageusia group on taste test; acute-phase self-reported dysgeusia also recorded; results reported as hypogeusia)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named: ODOFIN Taste Strips 50 (ODOFIN), total score 0-16, hypogeusia identified by a test score lower than 9
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Hypogeusia at Visit 1: total 27 (22.5%) of 120 (Group 1: 10 (25.0%), Group 2: 12 (30.0%), Group 3: 5 (12.5%)); at Visit 2: total 18 (15.0%) (Group 1: 7 (17.5%), Group 2: 6 (15.0%), Group 3: 5 (12.5%)) (Table 1)
onset_timing: not reported (enrolment was at 3, 6 or 12 months after viral clearance)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: Hypogeusia in Group 3 (enrolled 12 months post-recovery): 5 (12.5%) at Visit 1 (12 months) and 5 (12.5%) at Visit 2 (15 months post-recovery, i.e. beyond 12 weeks)
taste_score_change_as_printed: Gustatory function score (mean +/- SD) total: Visit 1 10.77 +/- 2.73 to Visit 2 11.18 +/- 2.40 (Group 1: 10.75 +/- 2.92 to 11.13 +/- 2.45; Group 2: 10.82 +/- 3.15 to 11.40 +/- 2.49; Group 3: 10.72 +/- 2.06 to 11.03 +/- 2.30); two-way ANOVA revealed no significant main effect of recovery group or within-group differences on ODOFIN scores; abstract states gustatory function had largely normalised at the first visit across all groups and remained stable at follow-up
pathogenesis_finding: Plasma alpha-synuclein showed no significant correlation with gustatory function at either visit (V1: rho=0.061, p=0.533; V2: rho=0.067, p=0.494), and no other biomarker (Abeta42, GFAP, S100B, NSE, ferritin) correlated with gustatory function, suggesting gustatory function recovers independently of longer-term alpha-synuclein / protein-aggregation dynamics (T11)
special_populations_notes: Older adults: cohort mean age 59.9 +/- 8.6 years; age was a significant negative predictor of olfactory (not gustatory) performance in regression as printed; neurodegenerative disease excluded; no children/pregnancy/diabetes-specific taste results stated
follow_up_duration: Participants enrolled at 3, 6 or 12 months post-viral clearance and re-evaluated 3 months later; longest assessment Group 3 Visit 2 at 15 months post-recovery
funding_conflicts: Funding: Health and Medical Research Fund (HMRF) - Commissioned Research on COVID-19 from the Health Bureau of Hong Kong SAR (reference COVID1903007) and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (reference P0052607-ZZUA). Conflicts: authors declare no competing interests
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): recovery fields = not reported per R3 — the paper prints hypogeusia counts at each visit but no recovery proportions; extractor A had derived a 'reduction in prevalence' and quoted resolution statements as recovery/time-to-recovery, which R3 and the no-computation rule disallow (extractor B's position upheld). Pathogenesis per R5: T1 is the paper's taste-specific cited mechanism (viral replication within taste receptor cells; SARS-CoV-2 co-localisation with type II taste cell markers and ACE2 within taste buds); T11 is the study's own tested mechanism (plasma protein-aggregation/neurodegeneration biomarkers vs gustatory function, direct-human, null); sustentacular-cell infection (T2), chronic T-cell infiltration and microvascular injury (T8) passages in the Introduction concern the olfactory epithelium/bulb only — smell-only, not Q2-coded per R5; T9 not coded separately (protein-aggregation mechanism captured as T11). Directness mixed-as-stated (cited T1/T5 speculative; biomarker test direct-human). No intervention tested, Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: mechanistic human | single-cell transcriptomic analysis of salivary epithelial cells; long COVID with bitter taste dysfunction (LC-D) compared with healthy controls
country_setting: United States of America; Indiana University, Indianapolis, IN
N_total: long COVID cohort assessed for taste 42 ; scRNA-seq samples: 6 LC individuals with impaired bitter taste (LC-D) and 6 healthy pre-COVID controls
population_description: Adults aged 18 years and older from the IU School of Medicine COVID-19 Research Registry with self-reported taste loss following a positive test lasting longer than 60 days; LC cohort average age 51.7 +/- 14 years, male-to-female ratio 13:28, average BMI 29.7 +/- 6.7; most self-identified as White/European ancestry; healthy controls were cryopreserved pre-COVID saliva samples
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia; ageusia; phantogeusia (phantom or faulty taste perceived in response to blank strips)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named: Waterless Empirical Taste Test (WETT) (Sensonics International), 53 paper taste strips; LC-D defined as low bitter score <=1
taste_prevalence_as_printed: In the LC cohort (n=42): impaired bitter taste 30% (13/42), impaired sweet 29% (12/42), impaired sour 17% (7/42) and impaired salty 19% (8/42); complete ageusia was observed in 5% (no numerator printed); phantom or faulty taste was observed in 11.9% of individuals
onset_timing: not reported (eligibility required self-reported taste loss lasting longer than 60 days after the positive test)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (persistence described qualitatively as taste dysfunction persisting for months to years in long COVID; no proportion at >=12 weeks printed)
taste_score_change_as_printed: not reported (taste score distributions shown in Figure 2 only; no numeric score change printed)
pathogenesis_finding: Salivary epithelial cell transcriptomes from LC-D individuals showed downregulation of Type II and III taste receptor genes critical for bitter taste perception and of genes involved in cytoskeletal dynamics and taste cell-nerve synapse assembly, with TLR2 and TLR4 downregulated suggesting chronic inflammation, supporting a model of sustained dysregulated epithelial turnover in LC-D (8472 cells sequenced; 7321 cells post-QC)
special_populations_notes: none reported (new-onset diabetes is mentioned only in Introduction as a possible co-morbid risk of impaired taste sensitivity in long COVID, not as a characteristic or result for this cohort)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Delta Dental Research Program to MS, grant number #44-762-54; funders had no role in design, collection, analyses, interpretation, writing or decision to publish. Conflicts: authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): design is a human mechanistic single-cell transcriptomic study of salivary epithelial cells (SECs), not a prevalence cohort: the 42-person LC cohort provides the taste-test percentages and 12 samples (6 LC-D with bitter taste scores <=1, 6 healthy controls) provide the scRNA-seq data. Verbatim definition: 'Individuals with a history of a SARS-CoV-2-positive laboratory (RT-PCR) test and self-reported taste loss following the positive test lasting for longer than 60 days were recruited. This included 42 individuals.' Mechanism mapped to T1 (taste receptor cells), T3 (taste cell-nerve synapse) and T5 (chronic inflammation); no salivary-gland dysfunction (T6) claim was made for tastant delivery, so T6 not coded. No intervention was administered, so Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: case-control | participants divided into OGD group (cases with olfactory/gustatory dysfunction) and no-OGD group (controls); 50 and 50 recruited by design
country_setting: Bosnia and Herzegovina; University of Sarajevo, Institute for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology
N_total: recruited 100 unrelated individuals ; analysed 96 (4 samples excluded due to low genotyping quality following NGS)
population_description: Unrelated, nonclinical healthy adult volunteers aged over 18 years with confirmed COVID-19 infection at least once during 2020-2022; 50 males and 50 females in the recruited cohort of 100; largest age bracket 18-39 years (69.79% of the total analysed cohort); no chronic diseases in personal medical history (inclusion criterion); analysed groups OGD n=48 and no-OGD n=48
taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (38-question survey adapted based on MCSTQ-Sc; self-reported taste dysfunction used to divide groups; grouping phenotype was combined olfactory and gustatory dysfunction (OGD))
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: cohort divided by design with 50 individuals with OGD and 50 without dysfunction of 100 recruited (48 and 48 in the analysed cohort, total 96); taste-specific prevalence not printed in the text (specific loss patterns shown only in Figure 2); Discussion states for ageusia: 'The 15% incidence observed here' (no numerator/denominator printed for that figure)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (Introduction cites other studies for persistent OGD at 6 months; no persistent proportion from this cohort printed)
pathogenesis_finding: Statistically significant differences (BH-adjusted p=0.030 for all) were observed for HCN4 variants c.*2393C>G (p=0.013) and c.2556G>A (p=0.026), PLCB2 variants c.3037-55T>C (p=0.019) and c.582+958_582+959inv (p=0.021), and TAS1R1 variant c.1594+41G>A (p=0.03), indicating possible association of taste-signalling gene variants (T11: host genetic susceptibility) with taste dysfunction in response to virus infection
special_populations_notes: Children excluded (age under 18 years was an exclusion criterion); chronic diseases excluded (presence of chronic diseases was an exclusion criterion and no chronic diseases in personal medical history was an inclusion criterion)
funding_conflicts: Funding: grant of the Ministry of Science, Higher Education and Youth of Sarajevo Canton (contract no.: 27-02-11-41250-40/21). Conflicts: authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): prevalence carries the BY-DESIGN SAMPLING prefix per R2 (case-control sampling by OGD status); the 48/96 split must not be read as a taste prevalence. Taste-ambiguous resolution: the case/control grouping was the composite OGD phenotype (smell and/or taste); Figure 2 shows loss-of-smell only, loss-of-taste only and loss of both patterns but the percentages are in the figure only, so the only taste-specific prevalence in text is the Discussion's 15% ageusia incidence. Pathogenesis per R5: Introduction proposes damage to taste buds mediated by infection/inflammation and dysfunction of supporting nonneuronal cells extended to taste mucosa (T1/T2), cytokine-storm secondary damage via ACE2 expression within taste buds (T5); the study's own new evidence is genetic (T11, direct-human), hence directness mixed-as-stated. Confirmation verbatim: inclusion required 'confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in the past year by a primary care physician after the PCR test'. No intervention was tested, so Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: cross-sectional | cross-sectional online survey, quota-balanced across age and sex, conducted January 2025

onset_timing: not reported (respondents with an identifiable cause attributed onset to a post-infectious event following an upper respiratory tract infection; no onset timing printed)

funding_conflicts: Funding: Funding was received via the Rosetrees Trust (as printed, spelling 'recieved' in original). Conflicts: authors have no conflicts of interest to declare
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): virus = unspecified possible viral — a general-population SATD survey of mixed aetiology, not a confirmed-virus cohort; among 454 respondents providing suspected aetiology, all (100%) indicated symptoms began following an acute upper respiratory tract infection such as a cold, influenza, or COVID-19, by self-report with no laboratory confirmation. No intervention was administered or tested (treatments in the Discussion are cited literature/expert consensus only), so Q3 fields blank per R6 ('Q3-tagged, no intervention tested'). Pathogenesis discussion (miswiring hypothesis) concerns olfactory parosmia/phantosmia, not taste — general/olfactory mechanism not taste-extended, not Q2-coded per R5, so Q2 fields blank.

design: cross-sectional | multicenter, observational, analytical cross-sectional study (as stated)
country_setting: Spain; Region of Murcia, multicenter (Virgen de la Arrixaca University Clinical Hospital and collaborating centers)
N_total: original pool 201 adults with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection ; final analysis 104

taste_measurement: self-report symptom yes-no (olfactory dysfunction and dysgeusia recorded as dichotomous/binary present-absent variables; participants asked at the post-acute visit whether they had experienced gustatory dysfunction at any time during their COVID-19 illness)
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Dysgeusia reported by 36.5% (n=38) of 104 participants; alterations in taste perception were absent in 63.5% (n=66)
onset_timing: not reported (paper states: 'Detailed information regarding symptom onset, duration, or progression during the acute phase was not collected')
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: not reported (assessment was at approximately 75 days after diagnosis but asked about occurrence at any time during illness, not persistence at that visit)
pathogenesis_finding: No statistically significant associations were observed between expression levels of ACE2, TMPRSS2, furin or NRP1 (quantified in nasal and/or pharyngeal samples approximately 75 days after diagnosis) and the presence of dysgeusia in adjusted continuous models (furin OR=1.23, p=0.319; ACE2 OR=1.04, p=0.115; NRP1 OR=1.01, p=0.195; TMPRSS2 OR=1.17, p=0.506) or tertile models, supporting a multifactorial model rather than direct determination by isolated baseline receptor expression
special_populations_notes: none reported (models adjusted for age, sex and race as stated; no pregnancy, children, diabetes, CKD/liver, immunocompromised or pre-existing chemosensory disorder results stated for taste)
follow_up_duration: not reported (single post-acute study visit approximately 75 days after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection; no longitudinal follow-up)
funding_conflicts: Funding: this research received no external funding (as printed). Conflicts: authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): follow_up_duration = not reported — the ~75-day visit is a single cross-sectional assessment, not follow-up (extractor A had entered the visit timing as follow-up). Verbatim scope statement: 'The aim of this assessment was not to characterize the clinical features, severity, timing, or evolution of these symptoms.' Pathogenesis per R5: T1 = high ACE2/TMPRSS2/furin expression in oral mucosal epithelium and taste cells suggesting viral entry and direct sensory damage (cited studies); T3 = direct/indirect viral invasion / retrograde transport discussed for gustatory-relevant pathways; T5 = inflammatory processes. T2 NOT coded: the sustentacular/glial-cell passage states ACE2/TMPRSS2 are 'predominantly expressed in nonneuronal cells of the olfactory epithelium, such as sustentacular and glial cells, suggesting that olfactory damage is mediated mainly by inflammatory and indirect mechanisms' — smell-only, not taste-extended (extractor A had coded T2). This study's own evidence is direct human receptor-expression measurement with a null association for dysgeusia. No intervention tested, Q3 fields blank per R6.

design: case-control | single-center retrospective case-control study (as stated in title and Methods)
country_setting: Japan; Kanagawa Cancer Center Hospital, Yokohama
N_total: admitted with COVID-19 520 ; met inclusion/exclusion criteria (baseline cohort) 95 ; analysed 52 (26 patients with dysosmia/dysgeusia (group A) and 26 matched patients without these symptoms (group B))
virus_confirmation: laboratory-confirmed (nucleic acid test or antigen quantitative test)
population_description: Inpatients admitted with acute COVID-19 between September 13 2021 and September 30 2023 at a cancer center hospital, including regular patients with cancer and referred patients; group A mean age 52.77 years, group B mean age 51.85 years; group A sex M:F=10:16, group B M:F=15:11; controls matched for post-day from onset, age, COVID-19 severity and proportion of patients with cancer
taste_types_reported: dysgeusia; ageusia; hypogeusia; hypergeusia (including hypersensitivity to salty taste and hypersensitivity to bitter taste, and hyper-sensation for salty/sour, as listed per patient in Table 1)
taste_measurement: other-as-stated: structured checklist interview by a COVID-19 specialist physician or duty nurses during hospital admission (presence/absence of symptoms; taste sensation evaluated after consumption of hospital-provided food for sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami); symptoms were chief complaints at admission confirmed by the attending physician; paper states evaluation lacked standardized validated tools
taste_prevalence_as_printed: BY-DESIGN SAMPLING: not reported as a cohort prevalence (case-control by design: 26 with dysosmia and/or dysgeusia (group A) selected from 95 eligible patients, 26 matched without (group B)). Dysgeusia manifestations in group A were 'primarily ageusia or hypogeusia, followed by hypersensitivity to salty taste' (individual manifestations listed per patient in Table 1); Table 3 (50 patients with known vaccination status): dysgeusia positive in 6 unvaccinated and 15 vaccinated patients, negative in 5 and 24 respectively (Fisher's p=0.340)
onset_timing: Dysosmia/dysgeusia were chief complaints at admission in group A; blood sampling at mean post-day from onset (pdo) 4.69 +/- 2.51 days in group A vs 3.62 +/- 2.22 days in group B (abstract; Results text/Table 2 give 4.69 +/- 2.56 and 3.62 +/- 2.26)
pathogenesis_finding: Group A (dysosmia/dysgeusia) had significantly lower serum tryptophan [median 9.70 ug/mL (range 4.59-13.89) vs 10.40 (7.52-13.34), p=0.031] and higher kynurenine-tryptophan ratio (KTR) [61.34 (40.47-384.2) vs 53.52 (26.13-86.64)] and quinolinic acid (QUIN) [574.39 nM (100.39-11909) vs 443.65 (83.09-998.3)] than group B, with no significant differences in 5-HT or kynurenic acid, suggesting serum KTR and QUIN may serve as biomarkers for dysgeusia/dysosmia during acute COVID-19 (T11: kynurenine pathway / tryptophan metabolite neuroimmune imbalance; T5: inflammation-driven IDO/TDO activity)
special_populations_notes: Pregnancy: pregnant women were excluded; children/adolescents aged <20 years excluded; pre-existing taste or smell impairment excluded; current smokers excluded; cancer: patients with cancer included (14/26 (53.85%) in group A), but recent anti-cancer chemotherapy within three weeks before infection, untreated/incompletely treated brain metastases or CNS invasion, and pre-existing impairment due to cancer/therapy were excluded; CKD: one group A outlier (patient A-11) had prolonged renal dysfunction following anti-cancer therapy noted in Discussion
follow_up_duration: not reported (acute-phase, admission/blood sampling at <5 days from onset as targeted; no follow-up duration stated)
funding_conflicts: Funding: Kanagawa Prefecture Hospital Cancer Fund [grant number 2022CancerC358]; funder had no role in study design, collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or decision to submit. Conflicts: Jun Tsukiji reports receiving a scholarship from Shionogi Pharma (the Kanagawa Prefecture Hospital Cancer Fund [grant number 2022CancerC358]); other authors declare no conflicts of interest
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): prevalence carries the BY-DESIGN SAMPLING prefix per R2 (retrospective case-control sampled by symptom status). Pathogenesis per R5: the paper's proposed and tested taste mechanism is kynurenine-pathway neuroimmune imbalance (T11) driven by inflammation-regulated IDO/TDO activity (T5), measured directly in human serum by symptom group — direct-human. Extractor A's T3/T9 derive from background anatomy (peripheral chemoreceptors 'directly innervating central nerves') and general QUIN neurotoxicity discussion, not from a cranial-nerve or central gustatory mechanism proposed for the taste finding — not coded. P-value discrepancy within the paper: Abstract gives KTR p<0.037 and QUIN p<0.0169, while Table 2 Mann-Whitney p values are KTR 0.037, QUIN 0.044 and Trp 0.030 (abstract Trp p=0.031); both versions retained without recomputation. Combined dysosmia/dysgeusia grouping: biomarkers were compared for the combined group A, not for dysgeusia alone. No treatment was administered for taste dysfunction ('targeting kynurenine pathway' is proposed as a future therapeutic target only; zinc was only a measured laboratory parameter), so Q3 fields blank per R6 ('Q3-tagged, no intervention tested').

design: case series >=10 | retrospective study (paper's wording); single-arm pre-post treatment follow-up with no control group
country_setting: Taiwan; Taichung Veterans General Hospital outpatient clinic; Omicron prevalent period
N_total: enrolled 71 long COVID patients (34 complained of smell and taste loss; 36 complained only of smell loss; 1 complained only of taste loss)
population_description: Long COVID patients with persistent loss of smell and/or taste for >1 month after infection, infected between March 2022 and August 2023 (Results) / enrolled May 2022-December 2023 (Methods), who had normal olfactory and gustatory function preinfection; smell+taste group ages 20-73 years, mean 38.35 +/- 15.44 years, 11 male and 23 female; smell-only group ages 22-69 years, mean 44.92 +/- 14.20 years; the taste-only patient was a 71-year-old woman
taste_types_reported: hypogeusia (objective gustatory dysfunction on WETT); unspecified taste dysfunction (complaint of taste loss)
taste_measurement: validated gustatory test named: Waterless Empirical Taste Test (WETT), 40-point maximum for correct quality identification; normative WETT values established at 16 for male adults and 23 for female adults as printed; plus telephone self-report at follow-up
taste_prevalence_as_printed: Among the 34 patients complaining of smell and taste loss, WETT showed gustatory dysfunction in 8 patients (23.5%) at the first visit (normal in 26). Among the 36 patients complaining only of smell loss, WETT showed gustatory dysfunction in 6 patients (16.7%) at the first visit. Only one patient complained of taste loss alone (WETT score 1 at first visit)
onset_timing: Persistent loss for >1 month (at least 1 month) before enrolment; interval between SARS-CoV-2 infection and first outpatient visit ranged 1 to 11 months (mean + SD: 2.48 + 1.95 months for all patients; 2.53 + 2.21 months for the smell+taste group; 2.47 + 2.72 months for the smell-only group)
persistent_ge12wk_as_printed: After 2-4 months of treatment, gustatory dysfunction remained in 3 of 18 retested smell+taste patients (16.7%); at phone follow-up at a mean of 10.35 months (>=12wk), 16/34 (47.1%) reported no complete recovery of gustation (Table 1 phone review)
taste_score_change_as_printed: Retested smell+taste patients (n=18 of 34): WETT scores ranged 14 to 37 (mean + SD: 26.28 + 7.13) before treatment and 10 to 39 (mean + SD: 28.61 + 8.38) after treatment; WETT scores increased significantly after treatment (p=0.019). Retested hypogeusic subgroup (n=3 of the 18): none showed improvement in the WETT score — gustatory improvement rate 0/3 (0%) (Table 1). Taste-only patient (n=1): WETT score increased from 1 to 31 after 2 months of treatment
pathogenesis_finding: Objective WETT testing showed gustatory dysfunction in only 23.5% of patients who complained of smell and taste loss, and the authors conclude most COVID-19 patients who complained of gustatory dysfunction did not really have a taste problem but had developed a flavor disorder associated with olfactory dysfunction (T4); other hypothesised mechanisms cited are indirect damage to taste receptors from infected epithelial cells and local inflammation (T1/T5), and ACE2 expression in taste organs after viral infection of the salivary gland (T6)
intervention: Oral zinc gluconate and oral steroids (prednisolone) (combination, single arm)
intervention_dose_course: Oral prednisolone (10 mg bid) and a zinc gluconate tablet (10 mg tid) were prescribed for a month; eligible patients then took another 1-3 months course of oral prednisolone and zinc gluconate (retest after 2-4 months of treatment in total, as reported)
comparator: pre-post none (paper states: 'we did not include control patients who did not receive medical treatment in this study')
N_per_arm: Single arm, no per-arm allocation: all 71 patients prescribed treatment as described; retested after 2-4 months: 18 of the 34 smell+taste patients and 21 of the 36 smell-only patients; taste-only patient (n=1) retested after 2 months
treatment_recovery_as_printed: Smell+taste group retested (n=18): gustatory dysfunction 3/18 (16.7%) after 2-4 months of treatment vs 8/34 (23.5%) at first visit in the full group; among the three hypogeusic retested patients, none showed improvement in the WETT score (gustatory improvement rate 0/3 (0%), Table 1), although the retested group's WETT scores increased significantly (p=0.019). Phone follow-up (mean 10.35 months, n=34): gustatory improvement 30/34 (88.2%) — 18 patients completely restored (complete recovery 52.9%), 12 partially restored, 4 without improvement. Taste-only patient: WETT 1 to 31 after 2 months of treatment; partial recovery of taste function by phone five months after the first outpatient visit
special_populations_notes: Older adults: the taste-only patient was 71 years old; sex- and age-specific test cut-offs/norms are printed, including for subjects aged >60 years (UPSIT-TC) and WETT minimal detectable change of eight for male adults and six for female adults. Exclusions: recent head trauma, diagnosis of autoimmune diseases, and sinonasal disease signs on nasal endoscopy (discharge, polypoid mucosa or polyps) were excluded; patients who reported complete recovery after the first month of treatment were also excluded from the study (as stated in Methods)
follow_up_duration: Objective retest after 2-4 months of treatment; phone follow-up at a mean of 10.35 + 5.50 months after the first outpatient visit (range 2 to 19 months) for the smell+taste group and 10.42 + 5.35 months (range 2 to 18 months) for the smell-only group
funding_conflicts: Funding: authors received no financial support for the research, authorship and/or publication of this article. Conflicts: authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship and/or publication of this article
extractor_notes: Settled (v1.1): design per R1(c) — pre-post treatment without a comparator and n>=10 is 'case series >=10', not a cohort; the paper's self-label 'retrospective study' is retained after ' | ' and the conflict is flagged here per R1(a). Recovery per R3: this is a single-arm treated cohort reported as a whole, so all recovery quantities sit in treatment_recovery_as_printed (field 25) and fields 13-15 point there — neither extractor's duplication into both blocks is retained. Taste score change (field 17) records BOTH printed quantities with subsets named: the retested smell+taste group change (n=18; 26.28 + 7.13 to 28.61 + 8.38, p=0.019) AND the retested hypogeusic subgroup result (n=3; 0/3 (0%) improved) — no WETT change is printed for the full 34-patient or 71-patient cohort. Pathogenesis per R5: T7 NOT coded — zinc is the Q3 intervention, justified only by a prior report of benefit in traumatic anosmia; no zinc-pathway disruption mechanism for taste is proposed (extractor A had coded T7). Directness mixed-as-stated: T4 is supported by the study's own human WETT data; T1/T5/T6 are cited hypotheses (speculative). Important design caveat printed in Methods: 'Any patient who had reported complete recovery from olfactory or gustatory function after treatment was also excluded from the study' before the second 1-3 month course, so the retest/phone cohort is selected for non-complete recovery after the first month. Abstract verbatim: 'After treatment, 77.8% of the patients were hyposmic, and 16.7% were hypogeusic.' No adverse-event reporting was located in the full text (adverse_events = not reported, as both extractors agreed).
